The first thing the town lost was its echo.

Children discovered this beneath the railway bridge, where they went to shout their names and hear the concrete shout them back. On Tuesday afternoon, a boy called Samuel yelled, “Hello!” and received nothing. Not even a small, embarrassed hello. His friends tried together. Their voices passed under the bridge and disappeared into the wet afternoon. They stood listening until someone suggested the bridge was broken, which seemed reasonable enough. Everything else in town broke eventually, and usually someone from the council arrived wearing orange and carrying a clipboard.

By Thursday, everyone had noticed.

The swimming pool sounded strangely intimate. Footsteps in the church stopped exactly when the feet stopped. At the station, announcements no longer dissolved into grand, incomprehensible thunder. People could finally understand which trains were late, though this improvement did little for public morale.

An acoustics professor visited from the university. She brought instruments in padded cases, made measurements, and frowned with professional restraint.

“Sound is behaving locally,” she told the mayor.

“Can you persuade it to behave normally?”

The professor requested a larger budget.

Then the town began losing other things.

Not objects. Objects remained stubbornly available. Keys were still found beneath newspapers; umbrellas accumulated behind café doors. What vanished were the small allowances people had never thought to name.

The comfortable silence between old friends disappeared. Two men who had fished together for thirty years suddenly found themselves discussing interest rates beside the reservoir. The feeling that a particular song belonged to a particular summer went next. People remembered the summers and recognized the songs, but the threads between them had been snipped.

Nobody knew which department should handle this.

At the municipal library, a woman named Mara started keeping a list.

She was the assistant librarian, though there had been no head librarian for eleven months. The council considered this an efficiency. Mara considered it a vacancy.

She wrote the missing things in a green exercise book: echoes; companionable silence; musical associations; the satisfaction of shutting a well-made drawer.

That last one had been reported by a carpenter who arrived near closing time and demonstrated with the catalogue cabinet.

“See?” he said, pushing a drawer home.

It closed perfectly.

“That used to mean something.”

Mara nodded and wrote it down.

At first, recording the losses seemed a modest public service. People felt better when someone believed them.

A woman reported that her dog no longer looked disappointed when she left for work.

“Isn’t that good?” Mara asked.

“I thought so. But now leaving feels exactly like staying.”

A baker had lost the conviction that the first loaf of the morning was special. A teenager said the view from her bedroom window no longer suggested that her life might happen somewhere else.

Mara made room for every report. Soon the exercise book was nearly full.

She noticed a pattern while shelving returned books.

Every missing thing had recently been described as useless.

The council had discussed soundproofing the railway bridge because children congregated there. An advice column had warned against unproductive silences. A popular article explained that nostalgia distorted judgment. The carpenter had complained that nobody would pay extra for a pleasing drawer when a cheap one held the same number of socks.

Mara searched local newspapers, meeting minutes, and public notices. The connections were not perfect. But they were numerous enough to keep her awake.

She took the exercise book to the mayor.

“Are you suggesting,” he said, “that the town is taking us literally?”

“I’m suggesting we’ve become careless about what we say we don’t need.”

He examined the list. Outside his window, workers were removing a crooked bench from the square. It faced neither the fountain nor the flowerbeds, but a patch of afternoon sunlight.

“That bench is being replaced,” he said.

“With what?”

“Nothing. It serves no clear purpose.”

They watched the workers lift it into a truck.

The mayor put on his coat.

They found the bench at the maintenance depot, between a cracked planter and several obsolete traffic signs.

The supervisor was reluctant to release it without paperwork.

“What purpose should I put down?” she asked.

Mara looked at the mayor. The mayor looked at the bench.

“Sitting,” he said.

“We have other benches.”

“Not there.”

The supervisor considered this, then handed him a form.

They returned it to the square before sunset. Nobody applauded. A man eating a pear asked them to move slightly left, out of the light.

Nothing happened that evening.

The following morning, Mara found three people waiting outside the library. One carried a half-finished jigsaw puzzle. Another wanted help remembering a joke her father used to tell. The third was the carpenter.

“I’ve made you something,” he said.

It was a little wooden box, empty except for a sliding tray. Mara opened it. The drawer moved smoothly, then settled with a soft, exact click.

For a moment she felt nothing.

Then she opened it again.

“Oh,” she said.

The carpenter sat down heavily on the library steps.

Recovery was uneven. Songs found their summers again, though not always the right ones. The fishermen managed twenty quiet minutes before one nervously mentioned a mortgage.

Mara kept recording things, now in two columns. The mayor stopped using the word “merely” in speeches. The crooked bench became popular, then unfashionable, then simply a bench again.

The echo returned in November. Samuel heard it first, answering a cough beneath the railway bridge. He ran to fetch his friends, who shouted until their throats hurt.

That night, Mara added one final note beneath the lists:

Returned. No further explanation available.

She nearly crossed it out. It sounded unfinished, and she preferred records that settled matters. Instead she left a little space below it, closed the exercise book, and placed it in the wooden box.

Outside, rain was beginning. Someone hurried past the library window carrying a coat above their head. Across the square, another person stayed on the crooked bench, watching the pavement darken around their shoes. Mara turned off the desk lamp. In the sudden quiet she heard the pipes knocking, a car starting, and the small click of the drawer as she pushed it shut with her thumb.
